intro: Every morning you put on shoes that crossed an ocean, eat cereal grown on soil that a glacier flattened, and walk to a school built on land that a river once drained. Geography is the study of where things are and why they are there. It starts with the planet itself: the grid of lines that gives every place an address, the plates that raise mountains and shake cities, the winds and currents that decide where it rains, and the rivers that tie a cornfield in Illinois to the Gulf of Mexico.

Then it turns to people. Eight billion of us live on a planet where most of the land is too dry, too cold, too steep or too wet to feed many people. So we crowd onto river plains and coasts, we move when a place fails us or another calls, and we trade for what our own ground cannot give. The map of languages, religions, farms, factories and shipping lanes is a map of those choices, made over thousands of years and still being made.

By the end of this unit you will be able to read a map and say what it hides as well as what it shows, explain why a place has the climate and the people it has, follow one ordinary object across the world, and argue, with evidence, about how people should use the land and water they share.
bigQuestion: How do the shape of the Earth and the choices of people together decide where and how we live?

test.q: A ship reports its position as 10 degrees south, 140 degrees west. What does the second number tell you?
choices: How far it is from the equator
How far it is west of the prime meridian
Which climate zone it is in
test.why: The second number is longitude, measured east or west of the prime meridian at Greenwich.

test.q: Why does a Mercator map make Greenland look as big as Africa?
choices: The projection stretches land far from the equator to keep directions true
test.why: Mercator kept compass directions straight, and the price was inflating high-latitude land.

test.q: Which is the best description of a projection?
choices: A photograph of Earth from space
A method for putting the round Earth on a flat sheet, which always distorts something
test.why: Because a sphere cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, every projection trades something away.

test.q: The east coast of South America fits the west coast of Africa, and the same fossils appear on both. Who first used this as evidence that continents move?
test.why: Wegener argued for continental drift from the fit of the coasts and matching rocks and fossils.

test.q: Where are most earthquakes and volcanoes found?
test.why: Plates meet at their edges, where the crust is squeezed, pulled or slid, and that is where the Ring of Fire lies.

test.q: Rome and Chicago sit at nearly the same latitude, but Chicago's winters are much colder. Which factor best explains this?
choices: Chicago is at a higher altitude
Chicago is closer to the North Pole
Chicago sits deep in a continent far from a warm sea
Chicago is in a rain shadow
test.why: Land heats and cools faster than water, so places far from the ocean have harsher winters and hotter summers.

test.q: Which biome has the most kinds of living things, and where is it found?
test.why: Hot, wet conditions all year make the tropical rainforest the richest biome on Earth.

test.q: Fertilizer washing off Illinois fields affects the Gulf of Mexico. Why?
choices: Illinois is in the Mississippi watershed, which drains to the Gulf
Illinois rivers flow into Lake Michigan
The Gulf of Mexico is part of the Great Lakes
test.why: Water from most of Illinois reaches the Mississippi and travels to the Gulf, carrying whatever entered it upstream.

test.q: Two cities are hit by the same size earthquake, and one suffers far fewer deaths. What most likely explains the difference?
choices: The luckier city was farther from the equator
Building codes, drills and warning systems in the safer city
Earthquakes are weaker near the ocean
The safer city had a lower population density
test.why: The hazard is natural, but the size of the disaster depends on how well a community prepared.

test.q: Which is the clearest example of a map being used as an argument?
choices: A map of Chicago's L lines
John Snow's map of cholera deaths around a water pump
test.why: Snow's map made a claim, that the pump water was the source of disease, without a word of text.

test.q: Why do almost all of Egypt's people live along the Nile?
choices: The river is the country's main tourist attraction
The rest of the country has too many mountains
The river provides the only large source of water for drinking and farming in a desert
test.why: Away from the Nile, Egypt is desert that cannot feed many people, so the population crowds along the river and delta.

test.q: Which of these is a push factor?
choices: A war that makes a village unsafe
A job opening in a Chicago factory
A cousin who already lives in the city
Good schools in a new town
test.why: Push factors drive people away from where they are; war is one of the strongest.

test.q: Which statement about resources is true?
choices: Renewable resources can never run out
A renewable resource can still be used up if taken faster than it grows back
Coal is renewable because more is always being formed
Countries with the most resources are always the richest
test.why: The Newfoundland cod fishery collapsed even though fish are renewable, because people took more than the sea could replace.

test.q: How did the shipping container change trade?
choices: It let goods move between ship, train and truck as one sealed unit, cutting costs sharply
test.why: Once handling became cheap, it became practical to make a product on one continent and sell it on another.

test.q: The Aral Sea, the Dust Bowl and the draining of Illinois wetlands all show which idea?
choices: Every human change to the land has effects, some of them unplanned, that must be weighed
Deserts spread no matter what people do
test.why: Each was a choice that brought gains and losses, often far from where the choice was made.

title: Geography of the World

chapters.title: Reading the World
chapters.bigQuestion: How do maps, plates, winds and rivers shape the world we live on, and how can we read them honestly?

story.title: Three Maps, Three Africas
story.kicker: Hang three world maps side by side and the same continent grows and shrinks before your eyes.
paragraphs: Imagine a classroom wall with three world maps pinned in a row. On the first, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. On the second, Africa is a giant and Greenland is a thin sliver near the top. On the third, the continents look like they might on a globe, but the edges of the world curve away like the sides of a football. Every map claims to show the same planet. They cannot all be right about the size of Africa. In fact, none of them is exactly right.

The first map is the one many people picture when they hear the word map. A Flemish mapmaker named Gerardus Mercator drew it in 1569 for sailors. On his map a ship's compass heading is a straight line, which is wonderful for steering across an ocean. The price is that land near the poles gets stretched wider and wider. Greenland covers about 2.2 million square kilometers. Africa covers about 30 million. Africa is roughly fourteen times bigger, yet on Mercator's map they look like twins.

The second map keeps every country's area in true proportion. Maps of this kind are called equal-area projections, and one of them, promoted in the 1970s by a German historian named Arno Peters, became famous. On it Africa and South America are huge and honest in size, but their shapes are pulled long and thin, like a reflection in a funhouse mirror. Sailors hate it. Some teachers love it, because it shows that the tropics hold far more land than the Mercator map suggests.

The third map, drawn by the American geographer Arthur Robinson in 1963, cheats a little everywhere so that nothing looks too wrong. Sizes are slightly off, shapes are slightly off, and the whole thing looks pleasant. Many atlases use it for exactly that reason. It is a compromise, and it admits it.

Here is the problem no mapmaker can escape. Earth is a ball, and a map is flat. Try peeling an orange and pressing the peel flat on a table. It tears, or it stretches, or both. Every flat map of the world must stretch or tear something. The mapmaker chooses what to keep true and what to sacrifice. That choice is a kind of argument. When you read a map, you are reading someone's decision about what matters.
story.think: If you were making a world map for a classroom in Chicago, which would you keep true, sizes or shapes, and who might disagree with your choice?

lessons.title: Latitude and Longitude
lessons.mainIdea: A grid of imaginary lines, latitude and longitude, gives every spot on Earth an address made of two numbers.
reading: A ship's captain in the middle of the Pacific sees nothing but water in every direction. How can she say exactly where she is? She uses two numbers. The first is *latitude*, how far north or south of the *equator* she is. The equator is the imaginary line that circles Earth halfway between the poles. Latitude is measured in degrees, from zero at the equator to ninety at each pole. Chicago sits at about 42 degrees north.

The second number is *longitude*, how far east or west she is. Longitude lines run from pole to pole like the sections of an orange. There is no natural starting line for east and west, so people had to agree on one. In 1884, delegates from many nations met in Washington and chose the line through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, England, as the *prime meridian*, zero degrees. Longitude runs from zero to 180 degrees east or west of it. Chicago is at about 88 degrees west.

Put the two numbers together and you have a grid address that no one can mistake. Chicago is roughly 42 degrees north, 88 degrees west. Every phone that shows a blue dot on a map is quietly using these numbers. Sailors used to find latitude from the height of the sun at noon or the North Star at night. Longitude was much harder, because it needs an accurate clock, and good sea clocks were not built until the 1700s.

One more thing to notice. Latitude lines are all parallel and the same distance apart, about 111 kilometers per degree. Longitude lines are not. They are far apart at the equator and meet at the poles. That is why a map that draws both sets of lines as a plain square grid has to stretch the polar regions, which is where our map troubles begin.

distance east or west of the prime meridian, measured in degrees from 0 to 180
the imaginary line around the middle of Earth, halfway between the poles, at 0 degrees latitude
the line of 0 degrees longitude, which runs through Greenwich, England

look.title: An Address With No Street
look.text: A hiker is lost on a prairie trail in central Illinois with no signs in sight. Her phone still works. It shows her position as 40.1 degrees north, 88.2 degrees west. She reads the numbers to a park ranger over the phone, and twenty minutes later a truck pulls up beside her.
look.prompt: Why could the ranger find her from two numbers alone, and what would she have needed instead if the grid did not exist?

check.q: What does latitude measure?
choices: Distance north or south of the equator
Distance east or west of Greenwich
check.why: Latitude counts degrees north or south of the equator, from 0 at the equator to 90 at each pole.

check.q: Why did nations have to meet in 1884 to choose the prime meridian?
choices: Because there is no natural starting line for east and west
Because Greenwich is at the center of Earth
Because ships could not measure latitude
check.why: The equator is a natural line, but any north-south line could be zero longitude, so people had to agree on one.

check.q: Longitude lines are far apart at the equator and meet at the poles. What problem does this cause for a flat map drawn as a square grid?
choices: Land near the poles gets stretched too wide
The map cannot show the equator
check.why: A square grid keeps the longitude lines apart at the poles, so polar land is pulled wider than it really is.

lessons.title: Why Every Map Lies a Little
lessons.mainIdea: Because Earth is round and a map is flat, every world map distorts size, shape, distance or direction, and the mapmaker chooses which.
reading: A *projection* is the method a mapmaker uses to move the round Earth onto a flat sheet. The word comes from an old idea. Picture a glass globe with a light inside, and paper wrapped around it. The lines of the globe throw shadows onto the paper. Move the paper or the light, and the shadows change. Every projection keeps some things true and warps others. There is no way around it.

Mercator's 1569 projection keeps directions true. A line of constant compass bearing is straight, which is why sailors used it for centuries. But it inflates the size of land far from the equator. Greenland looks as big as Africa when Africa is about fourteen times larger. Alaska looks larger than Mexico when Mexico is bigger. Antarctica smears across the whole bottom edge.

Equal-area projections, like the Gall-Peters map that became popular in the 1970s, keep sizes true but stretch shapes. Compromise projections, like Robinson's map of 1963, split the difference and are a little wrong everywhere. Even the choice of what goes in the center is a choice. Most maps put Europe or the Atlantic in the middle. A map centered on the Pacific, common in Australia and Japan, shows the Americas on the right edge, and it is just as correct.

So when someone asks which map is the real one, the honest answer is the globe. Every flat map is a tool built for a purpose. Ask what the purpose was and you will understand what the map keeps true and what it gives up. A good map reader asks that question every time.

words.d: a method for showing the round Earth on a flat map; every projection distorts something
the stretching or squeezing of sizes, shapes or distances that happens when a globe is flattened
a kind of projection that keeps the true size of land areas but changes their shapes

look.title: How Big Are They Really?
look.prompt: On a Mercator map Greenland looks about as big as Africa. Using the numbers, how many Greenlands would fit inside Africa, and why does the map get it so wrong?

check.q: Why must every flat world map distort something?
choices: A round surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing
check.why: Like an orange peel pressed flat, a globe's surface must stretch or tear when it becomes a flat sheet.

check.q: What did Mercator's projection keep true, which made sailors like it?
check.why: On Mercator's map a constant compass heading is a straight line, so a navigator could draw a course with a ruler.

check.q: A map centered on the Pacific Ocean puts the Americas on the right edge. According to the lesson, is that map wrong?
choices: Yes, because the Atlantic must be in the center
No, where the center goes is a choice, and it is just as correct
Yes, because the Pacific is too big to center
No, because Pacific-centered maps have no distortion
check.why: Where to center a map is a decision, not a fact. A Pacific-centered map is common in Australia and Japan and is just as valid.

lessons.title: Continents and Oceans
lessons.mainIdea: Earth's surface is mostly one connected ocean, broken by seven large landmasses we call continents.
reading: Look at a globe from above the Pacific and you see almost nothing but blue. About 71 percent of Earth's surface is ocean. Geographers usually name five oceans: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern around Antarctica, and the Arctic around the North Pole. Really they are one connected body of water. The Pacific alone is larger than all the land on Earth put together.

The land is divided into seven *continents*: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia. The word continent is partly a matter of custom. Europe and Asia sit on one solid piece of land, and some geographers call it Eurasia. Asia is by far the largest continent and holds well over half the world's people. Australia is the smallest, and Antarctica has no permanent residents at all, only visiting scientists.

Between the continents and oceans lie smaller features that matter to the people who live near them. A *peninsula* is land with water on three sides, like Florida or Italy. An island is land surrounded by water on all sides. A strait is a narrow water passage between two larger bodies, like the Strait of Gibraltar between Spain and Africa. A gulf or bay is where the sea reaches into the land, like the Gulf of Mexico.

Illinois has no ocean, but it does touch one of the largest bodies of fresh water on Earth. Lake Michigan is one of the five Great Lakes, which together hold roughly a fifth of the world's fresh surface water. Water from Lake Michigan eventually flows out through the other lakes, down the St. Lawrence River and into the Atlantic Ocean.

words.d: one of the seven largest landmasses on Earth
a piece of land with water on three sides
a narrow passage of water that connects two larger bodies of water

look.title: The Five Oceans
look.prompt: All the land on Earth covers about 149 million square kilometers. Which single ocean is bigger than all the land, and what does that tell you about how a globe looks from above the Pacific?

check.q: About how much of Earth's surface is covered by ocean?
check.why: Roughly 71 percent of Earth's surface is ocean, which is why the planet looks blue from space.

check.q: Why do some geographers say there are six continents instead of seven?
choices: Because Australia is too small to count
Because Africa and Asia are joined
Because Europe and Asia sit on one solid piece of land
check.why: Europe and Asia share one landmass, so some geographers combine them as Eurasia.

check.q: Florida has water on three sides. What kind of landform is it?
check.why: A peninsula is land with water on three sides. An island has water on all sides, and a strait is a water passage.

lessons.title: Plates That Move
lessons.mainIdea: Earth's outer shell is broken into huge plates that drift a few centimeters a year, carrying the continents with them.
reading: In 1912 a German scientist named Alfred Wegener stood in front of other scientists and made an odd claim. The continents, he said, were once joined and had drifted apart. His evidence was on the map. The east coast of South America fits into the west coast of Africa like puzzle pieces. The same kinds of rock and the same fossils of a small reptile appear on both sides of the Atlantic. Most geologists laughed. Continents plowing through solid ocean floor seemed impossible.

Wegener was right about the drift and wrong about the how. The answer came in the 1960s, when scientists mapped the ocean floor and found a chain of underwater mountains running down the middle of the Atlantic. New rock forms there as hot material rises from below and pushes the older floor outward. The floor spreads like two conveyor belts moving apart. The continents do not plow through it. They ride on it.

Today the idea is called *plate tectonics*. Earth's rigid outer shell, the *crust* and the top of the layer below it, is broken into about a dozen large *plates* and several smaller ones. Beneath them is hot rock that slowly flows, and heat from Earth's interior keeps it moving. The plates move a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Over millions of years that adds up to whole oceans opening and closing.

How do we know? Satellites can now measure the motion directly, and the numbers match what the rocks recorded. The Atlantic is getting wider by about two to three centimeters every year. If you could rewind two hundred million years, Africa and South America would slide back together, just as Wegener saw on his map.

words.d: the theory that Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that slowly move
one of the large, rigid pieces of Earth's outer shell
the thin, rocky outer layer of Earth

look.title: Wegener Reads the Map
look.text: Wegener argued that anyone who looked at a world map could see that the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together, and that the matching rocks and fossils on both sides were like the matching lines of print on the two halves of a torn newspaper page.
look.cite: Alfred Wegener, The Origin of Continents and Oceans, 1915 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Wegener had good evidence but no explanation for how continents could move. Why do you think most scientists refused to accept his idea for decades?

check.q: What evidence did Wegener use to argue that continents had once been joined?
choices: Matching coastlines, rocks and fossils across the Atlantic
check.why: Wegener pointed to the puzzle-piece fit of the coasts and to the same rocks and fossils on both sides of the Atlantic.

check.q: What discovery in the 1960s finally explained how continents move?
choices: New ocean floor forming at underwater mountain chains and spreading outward
The discovery of the Ring of Fire
check.why: Seafloor spreading showed that the ocean floor itself moves, carrying the continents along like a conveyor belt.

check.q: Plates move a few centimeters a year. Why can that still create whole oceans?
choices: Because the plates sometimes jump hundreds of kilometers
Because water pushes the plates faster
Because the crust is very thin
Because the motion continues for millions of years
check.why: A few centimeters a year over hundreds of millions of years adds up to thousands of kilometers.

lessons.title: Mountains, Quakes and Volcanoes
lessons.mainIdea: Most mountains, earthquakes and volcanoes happen where plates meet, because that is where the crust is squeezed, pulled or slid.
reading: Plates meet in three ways. Where two plates push together, the crust crumples upward. The Himalayas, the highest mountains on Earth, are still rising because the plate carrying India is ramming into Asia. Where plates pull apart, hot rock rises to fill the gap, as in the middle of the Atlantic and in the great rift valley of East Africa. Where plates slide past each other, they stick, strain and then jerk free. California's San Andreas Fault is a boundary of that kind.

That jerk is an *earthquake*. Rock along a *fault*, a crack in the crust, stays locked for years while the plates keep pushing. When the strain becomes too great, the rock snaps and the ground shakes. Scientists measure the energy of a quake with a magnitude scale. Each whole step on the scale means about thirty-two times more energy released. A magnitude 7 quake is not a little stronger than a 5. It releases roughly a thousand times more energy.

A *volcano* is a place where melted rock, called magma, reaches the surface. Most volcanoes sit along plate boundaries, especially around the edge of the Pacific Ocean in a belt nicknamed the Ring of Fire. Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, Alaska and the Andes all lie on it. Some volcanoes, like the ones that built the Hawaiian Islands, sit in the middle of a plate above a hot spot deep below.

Illinois sits far from any plate edge, so it is quiet most of the time. But not always. In the winter of 1811 and 1812 a series of huge earthquakes struck near New Madrid, Missouri, along an ancient buried fault. The shaking was felt across southern Illinois and rang church bells hundreds of kilometers away. The land there is still considered an earthquake risk today, which is why bridges and schools in southern Illinois are built to stricter rules.

words.d: sudden shaking of the ground when locked rock along a fault snaps free
a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock move past each other
an opening where melted rock from below reaches the surface
a number that measures the energy released by an earthquake

look.title: The Bent Fence
look.text: A rancher in California builds a straight wooden fence across a field. Years later he notices the fence has a kink in it. One half has shifted several meters sideways from the other, though no one moved it. The field lies across the San Andreas Fault.
look.prompt: What moved the fence, and why did the shift happen all at once instead of a little each day?

check.q: Why are the Himalayas still getting taller?
choices: The plate carrying India keeps pushing into Asia
Volcanoes keep adding lava to the peaks
Glaciers are piling snow on them
check.why: Two plates are pushing together there, and the crumpled crust keeps rising.

check.q: Roughly how much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 5?
choices: About a thousand times as much
check.why: Each step is about thirty-two times more energy, and two steps is thirty-two times thirty-two, roughly a thousand.

check.q: Where are most of the world's volcanoes found?
choices: Along plate boundaries, especially around the Pacific
check.why: The Ring of Fire around the Pacific follows plate edges, where magma finds its way to the surface.

lessons.title: What Makes a Climate
lessons.mainIdea: A place's climate depends mostly on its latitude, its altitude, its distance from the ocean and the winds and currents that reach it.
reading: Weather is what happens today. *Climate* is the pattern over many years. Chicago's climate has cold winters and hot summers, even if one January afternoon happens to be mild. Four things do most of the work in setting a climate. The first is latitude. Near the equator the sun shines almost straight down all year, so it is hot. Near the poles the sun's rays arrive at a low slant and spread over more ground, so it is cold.

The second is *altitude*, height above sea level. Air gets colder as you climb, by about six or seven degrees Celsius for every thousand meters. That is why Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania has snow on top even though it stands near the equator. Quito, the capital of Ecuador, sits almost on the equator but is cool all year because it is nearly three thousand meters up.

The third is the ocean. Water heats and cools slowly, so places near the sea have milder winters and cooler summers than places deep inside a continent. Ocean *currents* move heat too. The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic, which helps keep western Europe warmer than places at the same latitude in Canada. Chicago, far from any ocean, swings from below freezing to above thirty degrees within a single year.

The fourth is wind and the mountains that block it. Winds carry moisture from the ocean over land. When moist air hits a mountain range it rises, cools and drops its rain on the windward side. The far side, called the rain shadow, stays dry. The Cascade Mountains in Washington and Oregon are like that: green rainforest to the west, sagebrush desert to the east.

words.d: the usual pattern of temperature and rain in a place over many years
height above sea level
a steady flow of ocean water that moves heat from one region to another
the dry area on the far side of a mountain range from the wind

look.title: Two Cities, One Latitude
look.text: Rome, Italy, and Chicago sit at almost the same latitude, about 42 degrees north. Yet Rome's January is usually mild, with little snow, while Chicago's January is often bitterly cold. Rome is near a warm sea. Chicago sits in the middle of a continent, though it does have a big lake beside it.
look.prompt: Latitude is the same, so what else explains the difference? Which of the four climate factors are at work here?

check.q: Why is it hot near the equator and cold near the poles?
choices: The equator is closer to the sun
Wind blows heat away from the poles
Sunlight hits the equator nearly straight down and the poles at a low slant
check.why: Slanting rays spread the same energy over more ground, so the poles get less warmth per square meter.

check.q: Quito, Ecuador, is on the equator but cool all year. Why?
choices: It sits nearly three thousand meters above sea level
It is near the South Pole
A cold ocean current flows past it
It lies in a rain shadow
check.why: Air cools by roughly six or seven degrees Celsius per thousand meters, so a high city stays cool even at the equator.

check.q: What would you expect on the far side of a mountain range from the ocean wind?
choices: Dry land in a rain shadow
Colder winters than on the windward side
check.why: Moist air drops its rain climbing the windward side, so the far side gets dry, sinking air.

lessons.title: Climate Zones of the World
lessons.mainIdea: Geographers sort the world into climate zones, from tropical to polar, that repeat in bands from the equator toward the poles.
reading: Around 1900 a German-Russian scientist named Wladimir Köppen noticed that the plants growing in a place tell you its climate. Where palms grow it is always warm. Where only mosses and small shrubs grow it is cold. He used temperature and rainfall to draw a world map of climate zones, and geographers still use a version of his map today.

The main zones run roughly in bands. *Tropical* climates near the equator are warm all year, some rainy every month and some with a wet and a dry season. Dry climates, deserts and the grasslands around them, get little rain, and many sit around 20 to 30 degrees north and south, where sinking air keeps skies clear. The Sahara, the deserts of Australia and the American Southwest are all in those bands.

*Temperate* climates have real seasons, with warm summers and cool or cold winters. Most of the United States, Europe, China and Japan are temperate. Illinois has a temperate climate with a sharp difference between seasons because it is far from the ocean. Farther north come the cold climates with long winters, like most of Canada and Russia, and finally the *polar* climates, where the warmest month never gets above ten degrees Celsius.

Mountains break the pattern. A tall peak in the tropics can pass through every zone on the way up, from rainforest at the base to ice at the top. That is why climate maps show highland zones as their own color. A zone is a useful label, but the real world is patchier than any map.

words.d: the warm climate zone near the equator, hot all year
the middle climate zone with warm summers and cool or cold winters
the coldest climate zone, near the poles, where even summer stays cold

look.title: Reading a Backyard
look.text: You are handed a photo of an unknown backyard with no caption. There are palm trees, a bright sun, thick green bushes, and puddles on the ground. Another photo shows short brown grass, a cactus, a bare rocky hill and a cloudless sky.
look.prompt: Using Köppen's idea, what climate zone might each photo come from, and what clues in the plants gave it away?

check.q: What did Köppen use as a clue to a place's climate?
check.why: Köppen saw that the natural plants of a place reflect its temperature and rainfall over many years.

check.q: Why do many of the world's deserts lie around 20 to 30 degrees north and south?
choices: Because those bands are closest to the sun
Because there are no oceans there
Because volcanoes dry out the land
Because sinking air keeps the skies clear and dry
check.why: Air that rose at the equator sinks in those bands, and sinking air brings few clouds and little rain.

check.q: Which climate zone does most of Illinois belong to?
check.why: Illinois has hot summers and cold winters, a temperate climate made sharper by its distance from the ocean.

lessons.title: Biomes From Rainforest to Tundra
lessons.mainIdea: A biome is a large community of plants and animals shaped by climate, and the same biome appears wherever the same climate does.
reading: Stand in the Amazon rainforest and you are in shade at noon. Trees rise thirty meters or more, and their leaves lock together into a roof called the canopy. It rains almost every day. A *biome* is a large region with a particular climate and the living things suited to it. The tropical rainforest is the biome with the most kinds of plants and animals on Earth. Rainforests grow in South America, central Africa and Southeast Asia, wherever it is hot and wet all year.

Move away from the equator and the rain becomes seasonal. The forest opens into *savanna*, grassland with scattered trees, like the plains of East Africa where zebras and elephants graze. Farther still the rain nearly stops, and you reach desert. The Sahara, the largest hot desert, stretches across northern Africa and is roughly the size of the United States. Deserts are not always hot. The cold, dry heart of Asia is desert too.

In the temperate zones, rain decides whether you get forest or grassland. Where rain is plentiful, forests of oak, maple and beech drop their leaves each fall. Where it is drier, grasses take over. Illinois was once mostly tallgrass *prairie*, a temperate grassland with grass taller than a person and soil deep and black from thousands of years of roots. Almost all of it is now farmland, which is the same rich soil put to a new use.

Farther north, the forest turns to spruce and pine that keep their needles through long winters. This is the boreal forest, or taiga, which circles the globe through Canada, Scandinavia and Russia. Beyond it lies the *tundra*, where the ground stays frozen a short way down all year and only mosses, lichens and low shrubs survive. Then comes ice. The same sequence, rainforest to tundra, repeats going up a tall mountain.

words.d: a large region with a particular climate and the plants and animals suited to it
tropical grassland with scattered trees and a wet season and a dry season
temperate grassland, once the main biome of Illinois
the cold, treeless biome near the poles where the ground stays frozen below the surface

look.title: Rain Makes the Biome
look.unit: millimeters of rain a year, typical
look.cite: standard rounded ranges from geography references
look.prompt: Tundra and desert get similar amounts of water, yet they look very different. What other factor besides rain separates them?

check.q: Which biome has the most kinds of plants and animals?
check.why: Hot, wet conditions all year let the tropical rainforest support more species than any other biome.

check.q: What was the main biome of Illinois before farming?
check.why: Illinois was mostly temperate grassland, the tallgrass prairie, whose deep black soil now grows corn and soybeans.

check.q: Why can you pass through several biomes while climbing one tall tropical mountain?
choices: Because rain increases all the way to the top
Because the plates move under the mountain
Because mountains are always in the temperate zone
Because the climate gets colder with altitude, just as it does toward the poles
check.why: Rising altitude cools the air the way rising latitude does, so the biomes change in the same order.

lessons.title: Rivers and Watersheds
lessons.mainIdea: Every drop of rain that falls on land belongs to a watershed, the area drained by one river system, and watersheds connect distant places.
reading: Rain falls on a cornfield near Peoria. Some soaks in. The rest trickles into a ditch, then a creek, then a *tributary* stream, then the Illinois River, then the Mississippi, and finally the Gulf of Mexico near New Orleans. The land that drains into one river system is that river's *watershed*. The Mississippi watershed is enormous. It collects water from thirty-one states, about forty percent of the land in the lower forty-eight, from the Rocky Mountains to the Appalachians.

Watersheds are separated by high ground called divides. The most famous in North America is the Continental Divide along the Rockies. Rain falling on its west side ends up in the Pacific. Rain on its east side heads for the Atlantic or the Gulf. Chicago sits on a much smaller divide. Water on one side flows to Lake Michigan and out to the Atlantic. Water on the other side flows to the Mississippi. The two are only a few kilometers apart.

The world's great rivers built the world's early civilizations. The Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus and the Yellow River all fed farmers with water and rich mud from floods. The Nile and the Amazon are the longest rivers on Earth, each about 6,500 kilometers. The Amazon carries far more water than any other river, about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans.

Because a watershed connects everything upstream to everything downstream, what one town does affects another. In 1900 Chicago reversed the flow of the Chicago River so that its sewage would run toward the Mississippi instead of into Lake Michigan, the city's drinking water. Cities downstream on the Illinois River were not pleased. Fertilizer washing off farms in Illinois today feeds a low-oxygen dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico. The river remembers everything.

words.d: all the land that drains its water into one river system
high ground that separates one watershed from another
a smaller river or stream that flows into a larger one

look.title: The Longest Rivers
look.cite: standard atlas figures, rounded; the Nile and Amazon are close and sources differ
look.prompt: The Illinois River is tiny next to these giants, yet its water reaches the Gulf of Mexico. How, and why does that matter for a town in Louisiana?

check.q: What is a watershed?
choices: A building where water is stored
The deepest part of a river
All the land that drains into one river system
A wall that holds back a flood
check.why: A watershed is the whole area of land whose rain and streams end up in one river.

check.q: Why did Chicago reverse the flow of the Chicago River in 1900?
choices: To send its sewage away from Lake Michigan, its drinking water
To stop the Illinois River from flooding
check.why: The city drank from Lake Michigan, so it turned the river around to carry waste toward the Mississippi instead.

check.q: Fertilizer from Illinois farms affects the Gulf of Mexico. What does this show about watersheds?
choices: Upstream actions reach places far downstream
Fertilizer travels only through the air
The Gulf of Mexico is part of Illinois
check.why: Everything that enters a watershed upstream can be carried all the way to the river's mouth.

lessons.title: Natural Hazards and Getting Ready
lessons.mainIdea: Natural hazards strike where geography puts them, and how many people they harm depends on how well a community has prepared.
reading: A *natural hazard* is a natural event that can hurt people: an earthquake, a hurricane, a tornado, a flood, a volcanic eruption, a drought. Geography decides where each one is likely. Earthquakes cluster along plate boundaries. Hurricanes form over warm tropical oceans and strike the coasts of the Gulf, the Caribbean and East Asia. Tornadoes are most common where warm, wet air from the Gulf of Mexico meets cold, dry air from the north, which is exactly the middle of the United States.

Illinois knows tornadoes well. On March 18, 1925, the Tri-State Tornado tore across Missouri, southern Illinois and Indiana for more than three hours. It killed about 695 people, more than any other single tornado in American history, and wiped the town of Murphysboro, Illinois, nearly off the map. Illinois also floods. In the summer of 1993 the Mississippi and its tributaries rose over their banks for weeks and drowned farms and towns across the Midwest.

The same event does not do the same damage everywhere. A strong earthquake in Japan, where buildings are built to sway and schools drill for quakes, often kills few people. A weaker quake in a poor city of unreinforced brick can kill thousands. The hazard is nature's. The disaster is partly ours. Building codes, warning sirens, weather radar, levees and evacuation plans all turn a deadly event into a survivable one.

Preparation is also about maps. Flood maps tell a family whether its house sits where the river will spread. Tornado shelters are marked on school maps. After the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004 killed more than two hundred thousand people, nations around that ocean built a warning system with sensors and sirens. The geography of danger has not changed. What changed is how much people know about it.

words.d: a natural event, like a flood or earthquake, that can harm people
a violent spinning column of air that reaches from a storm cloud to the ground
a raised bank built along a river to hold back floodwater
a series of huge ocean waves set off by an undersea earthquake or landslide

look.title: Same Storm, Two Towns
look.text: Two towns sit twenty kilometers apart on the same river. Both get the same week of heavy rain. In the first town, the river spreads across a park that was left empty on purpose, and no homes are wet. In the second town, houses were built right up to the bank behind a low levee. The levee fails and forty families lose everything.
look.prompt: Nature did the same thing to both towns. What choices made the difference, and what would it cost each town to make those choices?

check.q: Why does the middle of the United States get so many tornadoes?
choices: Because it is near a plate boundary
Because warm, wet Gulf air meets cold, dry northern air there
Because it is close to the ocean
check.why: Tornadoes form where very different air masses collide, and the central plains are where Gulf air and northern air meet.

check.q: Why can a strong earthquake in Japan kill fewer people than a weaker one elsewhere?
choices: Japanese buildings are built to sway and people drill for quakes
Japan is far from the Ring of Fire
check.why: Preparation, from building codes to practice drills, is what turns a hazard into a survivable event.

check.q: What was the Tri-State Tornado of 1925?
choices: A hurricane that hit three states
The deadliest single tornado in American history, which crossed southern Illinois
check.why: It ran through Missouri, Illinois and Indiana and killed about 695 people, more than any other single tornado in the United States.

lessons.title: Maps as Arguments
lessons.mainIdea: A map is never just a picture; someone chose what to show, how to color it and what to leave out, and those choices make a claim.
reading: In the summer of 1854 a deadly disease called cholera swept through a neighborhood in London. Doctors at the time blamed bad air. A physician named John Snow had a different idea. He walked the streets and marked every death on a map with a short black bar. The bars piled up around one public water pump on Broad Street. Snow's map argued, without a single sentence, that the water was the killer. The pump handle was removed, and the idea that disease could travel in water gained ground.

Snow's map made an honest argument. Maps can also make a misleading one. A map that colors whole countries a single shade hides the differences inside them. A map of election results colored by county makes a thinly settled countryside look like it outweighs a crowded city. A map with a bold red arrow makes an army look like it is already winning. Choosing the projection, the colors, the center and the title is choosing the message.

Maps have also been used to do harm. In the 1930s a federal agency drew maps of American cities, including Chicago, that shaded neighborhoods by how safe they were thought to be for home loans. Neighborhoods where Black families lived were colored red and marked as risky. Banks then refused loans there for decades. The practice is called redlining, and its effects on wealth and housing are still visible on maps of Chicago today.

So read a map the way you read an essay. Who made it, and when? What is it for? What does it show, and what does it leave out? Would a different projection, a different color scale or a different center tell a different story? A map cannot answer these questions for you. That is your job as its reader.

words.d: a deadly disease spread by dirty water, common in the 1800s
marking neighborhoods on a map as risky for loans, which shut out the people living there, often by race

look.title: Snow's Case Against the Pump
look.text: Snow wrote that nearly all the deaths had happened within a short walk of the Broad Street pump. In the few cases where a death occurred nearer to another pump, he found that the family had preferred the Broad Street water and gone out of their way to fetch it.
look.cite: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 1855 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Snow's map showed a pattern, but a pattern is not proof. What else did he do to make his argument stronger?

check.q: What did John Snow's 1854 map argue?
choices: That cholera spread through the water from one pump
That the disease came from the river
check.why: The deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump, pointing to the water as the source.

check.q: How can a map of election results colored by county mislead?
choices: It makes empty countryside look more important than crowded cities
check.why: Large, thinly settled counties take up more space on the map than small, crowded cities with far more voters.

check.q: What was redlining?
choices: A way of marking flood zones
Marking neighborhoods as risky for loans, which denied credit to the people there, often by race
A red line on Mercator's map
check.why: In the 1930s, maps shaded neighborhoods, often where Black families lived, as risky, and banks then refused loans there for decades.

review.q: Chicago is at about 42 degrees north, 88 degrees west. What do those two numbers describe?
choices: Its distance from the poles and from the ocean
review.why: Latitude gives the distance north of the equator; longitude gives the distance west of the prime meridian.

review.q: On a Mercator map Greenland looks as large as Africa. What is the real relationship?
choices: Africa is roughly fourteen times larger
Africa is about twice as large
review.why: Africa covers about 30 million square kilometers and Greenland about 2.2 million.

review.q: What finally convinced scientists that continents move?
choices: Mapping of the ocean floor showing new crust forming and spreading
review.why: Seafloor spreading, discovered in the 1960s, gave the mechanism Wegener lacked.

review.q: Which of these best explains why Mount Kilimanjaro has snow near the equator?
choices: It lies in a rain shadow
It is in the polar zone
review.why: Air cools with height, so a mountain nearly six kilometers tall stays frozen at its summit even in the tropics.

review.q: Which biome once covered most of Illinois?
review.why: Illinois was temperate grassland, whose deep soil is now farmland.

review.q: Where does rain falling on a field near Peoria eventually end up?
choices: The Gulf of Mexico, by way of the Illinois and Mississippi rivers
review.why: Central Illinois lies in the Mississippi watershed, which drains to the Gulf of Mexico.

review.q: A magnitude 6 earthquake hits two cities. One has strict building codes and drills; the other does not. What does the lesson predict?
choices: Both suffer the same damage, because the quake is the same
The prepared city suffers far less harm
The unprepared city suffers less because its buildings are lighter
Neither city is damaged at magnitude 6
review.why: The hazard is the same, but preparation decides how much of a disaster it becomes.

review.q: John Snow's cholera map and the redlining maps of the 1930s were both arguments. What is the main lesson for map readers?
choices: Maps made by doctors are always true
Every map reflects choices, so ask who made it and why
review.why: One map saved lives and the other caused harm, but both show that a mapmaker's choices carry a claim.

chapters.title: People, Resources and Trade
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people live, work and trade where they do, and what does one ordinary object reveal about the whole world?

story.title: The Long Walk of a Pair of Sneakers
story.kicker: The shoes by your door have already traveled farther than most people ever will.
paragraphs: Start with a cotton field. It might be in Texas, in India or in West Africa, where cotton grows in hot summers on flat, well-watered land. A machine or a pair of hands picks the fluffy white bolls, and a gin pulls out the seeds. Bales of cotton ride a truck to a port, and a ship carries them across an ocean to a spinning mill, where the fiber is twisted into thread and woven into cloth for the inside of your shoe.

Now follow the sole. It is mostly made from oil. Crude oil pumped in Saudi Arabia, Texas or Nigeria goes to a refinery and then to a chemical plant that turns it into a foam that is light and springy. Some of the rubber in the bottom comes from trees. Rubber trees grow best in the hot, wet climate of Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia, where workers tap the bark before dawn and collect the milky sap in cups.

The pieces meet in a factory, most often in Vietnam, Indonesia or China. Hundreds of workers, many of them young women who moved from farming villages to the city for the job, cut, glue and stitch dozens of parts into one shoe. The design, though, was drawn on a computer thousands of kilometers away, perhaps in Oregon or Germany, by people who never touch the cotton or the rubber.

The finished shoes are packed in a steel box the size of a small room, a shipping container. A crane lifts it onto a ship that may carry ten thousand such boxes. Three weeks later the ship docks in Los Angeles or Long Beach, California. The container rolls onto a train and heads east through the mountains and across the plains to Chicago, which handles more rail freight than any other city in North America. From there a truck delivers the box to a warehouse, and a smaller truck brings a single pair to your door.

Nobody planned that whole trip. No single company owns the cotton field, the oil well, the rubber trees, the factory, the ship and the railroad. Each step happened because someone, somewhere, found it worth doing. Geography set the stage: where cotton grows, where rubber trees thrive, where labor is cheap, where the deep harbors are, where the rail lines meet. The shoe on your foot is a map of the world, if you know how to read it.
story.think: Pick one object in the room. How many countries do you think touched it before it reached you, and which step would be hardest to move somewhere else?

lessons.title: Water, Soil and Coasts
lessons.mainIdea: People cluster where the land can feed them and where travel is easy: river valleys, rich plains and coasts.
reading: Look at a nighttime photograph of Earth taken from space. The lights are not spread evenly. They crowd along coasts, trace the paths of rivers and fill a few broad plains, while huge regions stay dark. Egypt is a clear example. Almost all of its more than one hundred million people live along the Nile River and its delta, a green ribbon in a brown desert. Away from the river the land cannot feed anyone.

Three things pull people to a place. The first is fresh water, for drinking and for crops. The second is good *soil*, especially the flat, deep soil of river valleys and old grasslands like the Illinois prairie. The third is access, a coast or a navigable river that makes it easy to move goods and people. The great cities of the world, from Shanghai to New York to Mumbai, almost all sit on a coast or a major river.

Places that lack these things stay thinly settled. Deserts, high mountains, dense rainforest and the frozen north hold few people. About half the world's population lives in East and South Asia, where monsoon rains and river plains have fed dense farming for thousands of years. Australia is nearly the size of the United States but has fewer people than Texas, because most of its interior is dry.

Chicago exists where it does for these same reasons. The site is flat and the soil around it is some of the richest on Earth. Lake Michigan gave it fresh water and a harbor. The short portage between the Chicago River and the rivers flowing to the Mississippi made it the natural link between the Great Lakes and the whole interior of the continent. Geography did not build the city, but it chose the spot.

words.d: the top layer of ground where plants grow; deep, dark soil grows the most food
the fan of low, rich land where a river spreads out and enters the sea
deep and calm enough for boats to travel on

look.title: Egypt at Night
look.text: From orbit, Egypt at night is almost entirely dark except for one bright line that runs north from the Sudan border and then spreads into a glowing fan at the Mediterranean Sea. The line is the Nile. The fan is its delta. Around it, for hundreds of kilometers in every direction, there is nothing.
look.prompt: What do the lights tell you about where Egyptians live, and what would happen to that pattern if the Nile ran dry?

check.q: Where do almost all of Egypt's people live?
choices: Along the Nile River and its delta
check.why: The Nile is the only large source of fresh water, so the population crowds along it.

check.q: Which three things does the lesson say pull people to a place?
choices: Fresh water, good soil and access by water
Flat land, cold winters and coal
check.why: Water to drink and farm with, soil to grow food, and a coast or river to move goods are the basic pulls.

check.q: Why does Australia, nearly as big as the United States, have so few people?
choices: Most of its interior is dry
check.why: Most of Australia is desert or dry grassland, so its people crowd onto the wetter coasts.

lessons.title: Counting the World
lessons.mainIdea: World population grew slowly for most of history and then very fast after 1800, and it is spread very unevenly across the land.
reading: For most of human history there were fewer people on the whole planet than live in the United States today. Around the year 1800 the world's *population* reached about one billion for the first time. Then it took off. Two billion came around 1927, three billion around 1960, and eight billion in 2022. The reason was not more babies. It was fewer deaths, as clean water, vaccines, better farming and modern medicine let far more children live to grow up.

Growth is now slowing. In many countries, including the United States, Japan and most of Europe, families have two children or fewer, and populations are aging. Most growth today comes from Africa and parts of South Asia, where families are larger and populations are young. Geographers study these patterns because they shape everything from how many schools a country needs to how much food it must grow.

Population *density* tells you how crowded a place is: the number of people divided by the land area. Bangladesh packs more than a thousand people into each square kilometer. Canada, one of the largest countries on Earth, has about four. Illinois has roughly ninety, but that average hides a lot. Chicago's neighborhoods hold thousands per square kilometer, while some downstate counties have fewer than ten.

A high density is not good or bad by itself. Dense cities can be efficient, with short trips, shared transit and lively streets. They can also be crowded, expensive and polluted. Empty land can mean freedom and quiet, or it can mean a long drive to the nearest hospital. What matters is whether the place can support the people who live there.

words.d: the number of people living in a place
how crowded a place is: the number of people per square kilometer or square mile
an official count of everyone living in a country, done in the United States every ten years

look.title: How Crowded?
look.prompt: Canada and Mongolia are huge and nearly empty. Using what you learned about climate and biomes, why might that be?

check.q: Why did world population grow so fast after 1800?
choices: People started having many more children
Fewer people died young because of clean water, medicine and better farming
check.why: Birth rates did not jump; death rates fell, so many more children survived to have children of their own.

check.q: What is population density?
choices: The number of people per unit of land area
The total number of people in a country
The number of cities in a country
How fast a population is growing
check.why: Density divides people by land area, so it measures crowding rather than total size.

check.q: Illinois averages about ninety people per square kilometer. Why can that number be misleading?
choices: Because the census is never accurate
Because Chicago is extremely dense while much of downstate is nearly empty
Because most of Illinois is water
check.why: An average blends a crowded city with sparse farm counties, so it describes neither one well.

lessons.title: Why People Move
lessons.mainIdea: Migration happens when push factors drive people out of one place and pull factors draw them toward another.
reading: In the early 1900s a young man in a village in southern Italy packed one bag and boarded a ship for New York. A young woman in Mississippi in 1917 bought a train ticket to Chicago. A family in Syria in 2015 walked toward the Turkish border. Each of them was a *migrant*, a person who moves to live in a new place. Geographers describe why with two words: push and pull.

*Push factors* are the things that drive people out. War, hunger, drought, floods, no jobs, unfair laws or violence against their group. *Pull factors* are the things that draw them somewhere else. Jobs, safety, land, schools, family already there, or simply the chance to be treated as an equal. Usually both are at work at once. The Italian villager was pushed by poverty and pulled by factory wages. The woman from Mississippi was pushed by racist laws and violence and pulled by Chicago's steel mills and stockyards, which were hiring.

That second story is part of the Great Migration. Between about 1916 and 1970, roughly six million Black Americans left the South for cities in the North and West. Chicago's South Side became one of their main destinations. They built churches, newspapers, businesses and the music called Chicago blues. They also met new barriers, from crowded housing to the redlining maps you read about earlier.

Migration changes both ends of the trip. The place people leave loses workers, often the young and ambitious, but gains money they send home. The place they arrive in gains labor, new food, new languages and new ideas, and sometimes tension with people already there. Chicago's history is a stack of such arrivals: Irish and German, then Polish and Italian, then Black Southerners, then Mexican and now many others. Each layer is written on the city's map, one neighborhood at a time.

words.d: a person who moves from one place to live in another
something that drives people to leave a place, such as war, hunger or lack of work
something that draws people to a new place, such as jobs, safety or family
the movement of about six million Black Americans from the South to northern and western cities between about 1916 and 1970

look.title: Letters to the Defender
look.text: In 1917 the Chicago Defender, a Black newspaper read across the South, printed letters from readers asking for help coming north. Writers described wanting steady work and schooling for their children, and asked whether a job and a room could be found for a family willing to do any honest labor.
look.cite: letters printed in the Chicago Defender, 1917 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Which push factors and which pull factors can you find in what these writers asked for?

check.q: A family leaves a village because a drought has killed its crops. What kind of factor is the drought?
check.why: A push factor is something that drives people out of a place, and a drought that destroys the harvest does exactly that.

check.q: What was the Great Migration?
choices: The movement of settlers west across the Rockies
The arrival of Irish immigrants in the 1840s
The move of farmers into Chicago after the 1871 fire
The movement of about six million Black Americans from the South to northern and western cities
check.why: From about 1916 to 1970, millions left the South for cities like Chicago, seeking jobs and escape from racist laws.

check.q: How can migration affect the place people leave?
choices: It loses workers but may gain money sent home
check.why: The home place loses labor, often its young people, but migrants often send money back to their families.

lessons.title: Culture Regions and Languages
lessons.mainIdea: Shared language, customs and history create culture regions whose borders on the map are real but blurry.
reading: *Culture* is the whole way of life a group of people shares: their language, food, religion, music, clothing, holidays and ideas about right and wrong. It is learned, not inherited. A baby born in Seoul and raised in Chicago grows up with Chicago's culture. Geographers draw *culture regions*, areas where people share many of these traits. Latin America, where Spanish and Portuguese are spoken and most people are Catholic, is one. The Arab world, from Morocco to Iraq, is another.

Language is the clearest marker. Roughly seven thousand languages are spoken on Earth, though most have few speakers and many are vanishing. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers. English is spoken as a first or second language in more countries than any other, a legacy of the British Empire and American influence. Spanish is the main language across most of the Americas south of the United States. Languages come in families: Spanish, French, Italian and Portuguese all grew out of Latin, which is why they share so many words.

Culture regions have no sharp edges. Along the United States border with Mexico, Spanish and English mix in the same sentence. In Switzerland, four languages are official. In India, the government recognizes twenty-two languages and hundreds more are spoken. A map that paints each country one color hides all of that. A better map would use many colors, and they would bleed into one another.

Chicago is a small map of the world's languages. Spanish is spoken in hundreds of thousands of homes. Polish has been common on the Northwest Side for more than a century. Chinese, Arabic, Tagalog, Urdu, Korean and dozens more are heard in neighborhoods, stores and schools. Your classroom probably contains more languages than some countries do.

words.d: the shared way of life of a group: language, food, religion, customs and beliefs
an area where people share many parts of a culture, such as language and religion
a group of languages that grew from one older language, like Spanish and French from Latin

look.title: One Word, Four Countries
look.text: The word for night is noche in Spanish, notte in Italian, nuit in French and noite in Portuguese. All four come from the Latin word nox. In German the word is Nacht and in English it is night, which sound alike too, but they did not come from Latin.
look.prompt: What does the pattern in these words tell you about where the people who speak them came from, and how might a geographer use words as evidence?

check.q: According to the lesson, is culture inherited at birth or learned?
choices: Learned from the people around you as you grow up
check.why: Culture is learned; a child raised in a place picks up its language and customs no matter where the child was born.

check.q: Why do Spanish, French, Italian and Portuguese share so many words?
choices: They were invented by the same king
They all grew out of Latin
They borrowed the words from English
check.why: These languages form a family descended from Latin, the language of ancient Rome.

check.q: Why does a map that colors each country one language hide the truth?
choices: Because countries change color every year
Because no country has an official language
Because many countries hold several languages, and they mix at borders
check.why: Switzerland has four official languages and India recognizes twenty-two; culture regions blur rather than stop at lines.

lessons.title: Religions on the Map
lessons.mainIdea: The world's major religions each began in a particular place and spread along the paths of trade, migration and empire.
reading: Every major religion has a birthplace you can point to on a map. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all began in the Middle East. Hinduism grew up along the rivers of northern India, and Buddhism began there too, when a prince named Siddhartha Gautama became a teacher around the fifth century BCE. Where a religion is today is a story of how it traveled.

Religions moved with people. Buddhism followed traders and monks along the Silk Road into China, Korea and Japan, and by sea to Southeast Asia. Islam spread from Arabia in the 600s and 700s with armies and then with merchants, reaching Spain in the west and, by sea, Indonesia in the east, which today has more Muslims than any other country. Christianity spread across the Roman Empire and, after 1492, across the Americas with European colonists and missionaries.

Today Christianity has the most followers, roughly two and a half billion, followed by Islam with roughly two billion. Hinduism has more than a billion, nearly all in India and nearby. Buddhism has several hundred million, mostly in East and Southeast Asia. Many people follow local traditional religions, and more than a billion follow no religion at all. Every count is a rough estimate, because belief is hard to count.

Religion shapes the landscape. It decides what buildings rise highest in a town, a church steeple, a minaret or a temple tower. It sets holidays, foods and rules about the week. It can bind people together, and it has divided them too, in wars from the Crusades to the partition of India in 1947. A geographer's job is not to judge any of it, but to see where it is and ask how it got there.

words.d: a person sent to spread a religion to new places
the network of overland trade routes that linked China with the Middle East and Europe for centuries
dividing a country into separate parts, as British India was split into India and Pakistan in 1947

check.q: How did Buddhism reach China, Korea and Japan?
choices: With traders and monks along the Silk Road and by sea
